# Psalm 105:23–45 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## Overview (Narrative Arc)

The psalm recounts Israel's history from the descent into Egypt through the Exodus, wilderness, and entry into Canaan — all highlighting God's faithful works. G. Campbell Morgan observes that the "master word in the psalm is the pronoun 'He,'" showing God's perpetual activity. David Guzik notes this psalm deliberately omits Israel's sins and rebellions; those are reserved for Psalm 106. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 23 — "Then Israel entered Egypt; Jacob dwelt in the land of Ham."

- **"Land of Ham"** is a poetic name for Egypt. Egypt (Mizraim) was a son of Ham (Gen 10:6), and the native Egyptian name was *Khem*, meaning "black," with reference to the soil colour. (Peake's Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/psalms-105.html)
- **"Sojourned"** — Jacob came not as a permanent settler but as a temporary resident. As a "stranger and sojourner," Jacob charged his sons not to bury him in Egypt but in Canaan (Gen 49:29). (Pulpit Commentary, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Spurgeon** paints a vivid contrast: "Shem the blessed came to lodge awhile with Ham the accursed: the dove was in the vulture's nest." He also notes: "He was hard to bring there. Perhaps nothing short of the hope of seeing Joseph could have drawn him to take so long a journey from the tombs of his forefathers." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps105.php)
- **Trapp** (quoted by Guzik): "Whither he feared to go, till God promised him his presence and protection, Genesis 46:3-4." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 24 — "And the LORD made His people very fruitful, more numerous than their foes."

- All commentators point to Exodus 1:7, 12, 20 as the historical referent: Israel multiplied explosively in Egypt. The Pulpit Commentary notes the Pharaoh himself admitted, "the people of the children of Israel are more and mightier than we" (Exod 1:9). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Gill**: "They increased the more they were afflicted, Exodus 1:12. So the people of God in this world sometimes increase in number, and that even amidst the persecutions of their enemies; as the Christians did in the first times of the Gospel under the Roman emperors." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/105.htm)
- **Spurgeon** calls this "an early instance of what has since become a proverb in the church — 'the more they oppressed them the more they multiplied.' It is idle to contend either with God or his people." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps105.php)

---

## v. 25 — "whose hearts He turned to hate His people, to conspire against His servants."

This verse is a major theological flashpoint because it says God *actively* turned Egyptian hearts to hate Israel.

### The Reformed / Calvinist Reading
- **John Calvin** insists the active reading is correct, not a passive "their hearts were turned." He writes: "The Holy Spirit unequivocally affirms…that the minds of men are driven hither and thither by a secret impulse (Proverbs 21:1) so that they can neither will nor do anything except as God pleases." He rejects the "middle-scheme" idea that "turned" merely means "permitted," calling it a distortion born of fear of what Scripture plainly says. Yet Calvin also safeguards: "the root of the malice was in the Egyptians themselves, so that the fault cannot be transferred to God." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11.xiv.vi.html)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: "God judicially dealt with them according to their perversity, in order that they might afford the opportunity for displaying His glorious power…God controls men's free acts." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-105.html)
- **Spurgeon** holds a nuanced position: God caused the hatred only in the sense that His goodness to Israel provoked Egyptian jealousy. "God cannot in any sense be the author of sin so far as to be morally responsible for its existence, but it often happens through the evil which is inherent in human nature that the acts of the Lord arouse the ill-feelings of ungodly men." He uses the analogy of the sun softening wax but hardening clay, or drawing foul exhalations from a marsh but fragrance from flowers. (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps105.php)

### The Arminian / Wesleyan Reading
- **Matthew Poole** (quoted in Spurgeon): "Not by putting this wicked hatred into them, which is not consistent either with the holiness of God's nature, or with the truth of his word…but partly by withdrawing the common gifts and operations of his Spirit…and partly, by directing and governing that hatred, which was wholly in and from themselves." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-105.html)
- **Pulpit Commentary** takes the softer line: "Not by direct action on their heart, but by prospering Israel until their jealousy was stirred." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

### Anglican / Broad Church Reading
- **Cambridge Bible for Schools and Colleges**: "The Psalmist does not shrink from attributing the hostility of the Egyptians to God's agency, because it was due to the blessings which He bestowed upon Israel; and inasmuch as it led to the Exodus, it was a link in the chain of God's action." (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/psalms/105.htm)
- **Ellicott**: "So the hardening of Pharaoh's heart is throughout the historical narrative ascribed to Jehovah. (Comp. Isaiah 6:9-10; Mark 4:12, &c.)" (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/105.htm)

---

## v. 26 — "He sent Moses His servant, and Aaron, whom He had chosen."

- Calvin calls Moses "the servant of the Lord" to teach that "he was not self-elected to his office…but, being the minister of God, executed the office with which he had been entrusted." Aaron is said to be *chosen* — "those who are engaged in active and useful service for the Church, are not prepared exclusively by their own exertions…but are stirred up thereto by God." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11.xiv.vi.html)
- Guzik notes the title "His servant" is a wonderful designation for Moses, and that God gave both men the ability to perform signs authenticating their work. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 27 — "They performed His miraculous signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham."

- "Land of Ham" again designates Egypt (see v.23). The Pulpit Commentary notes that Aaron generally performed the earlier signs (Exod 7:10, 19–20; 8:6, 17) and Moses the later ones (Exod 9:10, 23; 10:13, 22). The phrase "words of his signs" means the declarations that were confirmed by miracles. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 28 — "He sent darkness, and it became dark— yet they defied His words."

- **Major textual variant.** The Hebrew reads "they rebelled not against his word" (which the KJV, NKJV follow). But the BSB reading ("yet they defied His words") follows the LXX and Syriac, which omit the negative. The Pulpit Commentary says Cheyne "boldly cancels the 'not.'" If the "not" stands, it refers to Moses and Aaron faithfully obeying despite Pharaoh's rage, not to the Egyptians. Calvin takes it this way: "they were not rebellious against his words" commends Moses' and Aaron's courage. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11.xiv.vi.html; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Guzik**: The plague of darkness showed Yahweh's superiority over Ra (the sun god) and Nut (the sky goddess). (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- **Peake's Commentary** notes the contradiction: reading "they did not rebel" contradicts the writer's evident meaning; it should read "But they did not observe his words." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 29 — "He turned their waters to blood and caused their fish to die."

- The plague was aimed at Osiris (god of the Nile) and Khnum (guardian of the Nile). Calvin notes the severity: though Egypt was well irrigated, they were "parched with drought amidst abundance of water." (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11.xiv.vi.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 30 — "Their land teemed with frogs, even in their royal chambers."

- Calvin offers a vivid meditation: God "did not gather together an army to fight against the Egyptians…but brought forth frogs, which contemptuously trampled upon the pride of that haughty nation." God shows He "has no need of powerful hosts to destroy the wicked; for he can do this, as it were in sport." The plague was aimed at Hekt, the frog-goddess of fertility. (https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom11.xiv.vi.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 31 — "He spoke, and insects swarmed— gnats throughout their country."

- Guzik notes this was directed against the fly-god Uatchit. The Pulpit Commentary identifies the "swarms" as the dog-fly or a kind of beetle, and the "lice" (KJV) as gnats. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 32–33 — "He gave them hail for rain…He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees…"

- The Pulpit Commentary observes the sceptical objection that "Egypt had no vines" has long been abandoned. The hail "smote every herb" and damaged trees (Exod 9:25). Guzik notes this plague opposed Geb (god of the earth), Nepri (goddess of grain), and Anubis (guardian of fields). Clarke (quoted by Guzik) notes Psalm 78:47 also mentions this, though Exodus does not specifically mention vines and fig trees. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 34–35 — "He spoke, and the locusts came— young locusts without number. They devoured every plant…"

- Opposite Shu (god of the atmosphere) and Min (deity of the harvest). The Pulpit Commentary notes the locusts ate "all the fruit of the trees which the hail had left" (Exod 10:15). The psalm describes eight of the ten plagues, not in Exodus order — the focus is on God's power, not the hardening drama. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 36 — "Then He struck all the firstborn in their land, the firstfruits of all their vigor."

- The climactic tenth plague. Guzik notes this was the "final and greatest plague," from which households protected by Passover blood were spared. The phrase "firstfruits of all their vigor" (lit. "the first of all their strength") echoes Psalm 78:51. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 37 — "He brought Israel out with silver and gold, and none among His tribes stumbled."

- **"Silver and gold"**: The Egyptians gave Israel great riches (Exod 12:35–36), fulfilling Exodus 3:21–22. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- **"None…stumbled"**: The Pulpit Commentary renders it "there was not one that stumbled among their tribes" — probably meaning all who walked had supernatural strength; the feeble were carried. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Spurgeon** draws a sharp contrast: "See the contrast between Egypt and Israel — in Egypt one dead in every house, and among the Israelites not one so much as limping." (https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps105.php)
- **Matthew Poole** (quoted by Guzik): "Diseased or unable for his journey; which in so vast a body…was wonderful; but they all journeyed on foot, Exodus 12:37." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

### Prosperity / Word of Faith usage
Some prosperity-gospel and Word of Faith teachers have used this verse to claim that God guarantees physical health and wealth for believers, arguing that just as no Israelite was "feeble" at the Exodus, so Christians should never be sick. None of the mainline Reformed, Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, or Pentecostal sources I examined read the verse this way. They uniformly see it as a specific historical miracle demonstrating God's covenant power at the Exodus, not a universal promise of perpetual health. The passage's own context leads toward v.45 — the purpose was obedience, not personal comfort.

---

## v. 38 — "Egypt was glad when they departed, for the dread of Israel had fallen on them."

- The Pulpit Commentary cites Exodus 12:33: "The Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 39 — "He spread a cloud as a covering and a fire to light up the night."

- The pillar of cloud by day gave shelter from the desert sun; the pillar of fire by night gave light and protection from wild beasts. Guzik calls them "remarkable emblems of God's presence and care." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 40 — "They asked, and He brought quail and satisfied them with the bread of heaven."

- The "bread of heaven" is manna, given continuously from the wilderness of Sin (Exod 16) until the first Passover in Canaan (Josh 5:12). The quail were given at least twice (Exod 16:13; Num 11:31). Guzik notes that David's remembrance is "distinctly positive" — he omits the people's grumbling and unbelief. Maclaren (quoted by Guzik) says this is "without one disturbing reference to the sins and failures which darkened the forty years." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/; https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 41 — "He opened a rock, and water gushed out; it flowed like a river in the desert."

- Refers to the two rock-water miracles (Exod 17:5–6 at Rephidim; Num 20:8–11 at Kadesh). The Pulpit Commentary calls "like a river" a "poetical exaggeration" of Num 20:11, where "the water came out abundantly." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Adam Clarke** (quoted by Guzik) adds a curious personal note: "I can now add, that a piece of this rock, broken off by the hand of my nephew, E. S. A. Clarke, in the course of the present year [1822], now lies before me. It is fine granite." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 42 — "For He remembered His holy promise to Abraham His servant."

- God's faithfulness to the Abrahamic covenant is the driving motive for the whole Exodus-and-conquest narrative. The Pulpit Commentary states simply: "i.e. his covenant with Abraham to bring his seed into the Holy Land." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- Guzik: "God binds Himself by His promises, and regards them as holy." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown** sees a two-fold purpose in God's dealings: (1) faithfulness to His covenant, and (2) that Israel might obey. Disobedience, the Psalmist implies, is the cause of the Babylonian captivity (the probable original setting). (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-105.html)

---

## v. 43 — "He brought forth His people with rejoicing, His chosen with shouts of joy."

- The "bringing forth" here refers not to the departure from Egypt but to the entry into Canaan from the wilderness — naturally attended with joy and gladness. The joy belongs both to Israel and to Yahweh. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html; https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)

---

## v. 44 — "He gave them the lands of the nations, that they might inherit the fruit of others' labor."

- Guzik, quoting VanGemeren: "By right of conquest they freely inherited from the Canaanites cities, vineyards, orchards, cisterns, and all kinds of material benefits." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- Gill draws a parallel to the heavenly inheritance: "In like manner the heavenly Canaan is enjoyed by the saints without any labour of theirs; this inheritance is not of the law, nor of the works of it, it is the gift of God, Romans 4:14." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/105.htm)

---

## v. 45 — "that they might keep His statutes and obey His laws. Hallelujah!"

This verse is the psalm's theological destination. Every commentator emphasises that *obedience is the purpose of redemption*.

- **Guzik / Kidner**: "The final verse shows why grace abounded; not that sin might also abound, but (to quote a New Testament equivalent), 'that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit' (Rom. 8:4)." Guzik adds: "God…set them free not for the ultimate purpose of personal indulgence, but so they could observe His statutes and keep His laws." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- **VanGemeren** (quoted by Guzik): "The emphasis throughout the psalm lies on God's goodness…And as an afterthought, the author reminds God's people of their responsibility. Keeping the precepts of the Lord is, therefore, an expression of joyous gratitude for all the benefits the Lord has provided." (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-105/)
- **Gill**: "All this the Lord did for them, to engage them by his goodness to them to observe the statutes he appointed them…And this is the end of our spiritual and eternal redemption by Christ, and of our effectual calling by his grace and Spirit, that we be zealous of good works." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/105.htm)
- **Ellicott**: The whole psalm is "an elaboration of the charge so often repeated in the Book of Deuteronomy…'only if thou carefully hearken unto the voice of the Lord thy God to observe to do all these commandments'" (Deut 15:4–5). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/105.htm)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: "This was God's purpose. How far Israel was from carrying it out appears from the historical books generally, and perhaps still more from the writings of the prophets." (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-105.html)
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown**: The two-fold reason for God's dealings: (1) faithfulness to His covenant, (2) that Israel might obey. Disobedience is the implied cause of their captivity. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-105.html)
- **Matthew Henry**: "Having redeemed us with his blood, restored our souls to holiness, and set us at liberty from Satan's bondage, he guides and guards us all the way…He redeems his servants from all iniquity, and purifies them unto himself, to be a peculiar people, zealous of good works." (https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/psalms/105.htm)

---

## Summary of Denominational Distinctions

| Issue | Reformed (Calvin, Spurgeon) | Arminian/Wesleyan (Poole, Pulpit) |
|---|---|---|
| **v.25 "He turned their heart"** | Active divine sovereignty; God governs all human wills; yet fault remains with sinners | Permissive agency; God withdrew restraint or used circumstances that provoked natural malice |
| **v.45 Purpose of redemption** | All traditions agree: obedience/holiness is the goal. Reformed emphasises this as God's sovereign purpose; Methodist emphasises it as grateful human response to grace. |

Both Baptist (Spurgeon, Gill) and Pentecostal-charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik) sources read v.25 in a Reformed-friendly way, insisting on God's sovereign direction of all events while guarding against making God the author of sin. The main divide is between those who read "He turned their heart" as *direct sovereign causation* (Calvin) versus those who read it as *indirect permission through circumstances* (Poole, Pulpit).

---

**Note on Catholic and Orthodox readings:** The search results from newadvent.org, catholic.com, and oca.org did not return specific verse-by-verse material on this passage within the search and fetch limits. The older commentaries used (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Spurgeon) are broadly shared across Protestant traditions and would align generally with traditional Catholic exegesis on the historical narrative, though the specific Calvinist-Arminian framing of v.25 is distinctively Protestant.
